By checking sufficiency, the system can notice missing links and expand the subgraph while the answer is still being formed. The third decision is about faithfulness: does the final wording match the graph? Verification catches the kind of error where a model names a plausible author, venue, relation, or attribute that was not supported by the retrieved structure. This staged design works when each agent's judgment is better than treating retrieval as a one-shot lookup. It improves over the naive approach by making the system adaptive before retrieval, skeptical during evidence selection, and constrained before final output.
502.po: The payoff is a more dependable academic question-answering system over scholarly graphs. According to the abstract, experiments on heterogeneous graphs constructed from OpenAlex and DBLP show consistent gains over strong language-model baselines, graph-augmented retrieval systems, and simpler agent-based baselines. Practically, that means the system is better suited to questions whose evidence lies across author, paper, and venue structure rather than in one text snippet. It buys three capabilities at once: choosing a retrieval path that fits the query, expanding evidence when the first retrieval is insufficient, and checking the answer against graph facts before presenting it.
502.limits: The abstract supports the design and reported experimental gains, but it does not prove that the agents always choose the right traversal or sufficiency threshold. The method assumes the scholarly graph is accurate, current, and connected enough to contain the answer. Missing authors, incorrect venue links, incomplete citation records, or ambiguous entity names can still mislead retrieval and verification. It also assumes that expanding a subgraph adds relevant evidence rather than mostly noise. The experiments use OpenAlex and DBLP-derived graphs, so the abstract alone does not show how well the method transfers to smaller, messier, private, multilingual, or rapidly changing scholarly collections.

503.bp: This paper serves a visual search setting where the user has an example image but wants a changed version of it. The query has two parts: the reference image, which shows concrete visual evidence, and modification text, which says how the desired target should differ. A shopping user might like the shape in one product photo but want another color; a design user might want the same scene with a different object. The search system must retrieve the target image from a collection, not generate a new image. SDR-CIR focuses on training-free zero-shot composed image retrieval, where the system is expected to work without learning from task-specific examples. The problem matters because a large multimodal model can describe the desired target, but that description can lean too heavily toward the wrong semantics from the reference image. The paper treats retrieval as a ranking problem that must both add missing target cues and subtract misleading source-image influence.
503.wh: The hard part is that the reference image is useful and hazardous at the same time. It supplies visual facts that the text may not repeat, such as shape, layout, object type, or fine appearance. But many facts in the reference should not survive the requested change. Training-free zero-shot methods often ask a multimodal language model to reason through the image and text and compose a target description. That sounds natural, but the abstract says fuzzy matching makes the generated description prone to semantic bias relative to the target image. In plain terms, a description can contain extra meanings pulled from the source, omit target details that matter, or overstate a feature that only partially applies. Retrieval then turns that imperfect description into a similarity score, so the bias is not just a wording issue. It changes which candidates rise in the ranked list. The central tension is preserving useful reference evidence while preventing redundant or irrelevant reference evidence from dominating the target search.
503.naive: A smart beginner would ask a multimodal language model to look at the reference image, read the modification text, write a description of the target image, and then retrieve candidates whose image features are closest to that description. This is attractive because it needs no new training data and converts a mixed image-text query into ordinary text-to-image search. It fails when the generated target description carries source-image bias. If it repeats visual details that the user meant to change, candidates too close to the reference may rank high. If it leaves out useful source cues, candidates may match the text but lose the intended visual identity. Simply trusting the description treats all carried-over semantics as equally useful, even though composed retrieval needs some reference cues reinforced and others penalized.
503.ap: SDR-CIR's central move is to make the ranking score aware of source-image bias instead of treating the generated target description as neutral. First, it uses Selective CoT, a guided reasoning process, to make the multimodal language model extract only the visual content that is relevant to the modification text. That reduces visual noise before ranking begins. Then it applies Semantic Debias Ranking in two steps. The Anchor step fuses reference image features with target description features. This reinforces useful semantics from the source and fills in cues the generated description may have omitted. The Debias step separately models how much visual semantic contribution the reference image makes to the description, then uses that contribution as a penalty term in the similarity score. The method therefore does two opposite jobs: it restores source evidence that helps identify the desired target, while subtracting source evidence that would redundantly pull the search back toward the original image.
503.mech: The input is a composed retrieval query: one reference image, one modification text, and a collection of candidate target images. First, SDR-CIR sends the image and text through a multimodal language model with Selective CoT. CoT means the model is prompted to reason in intermediate steps; selective means those steps are constrained toward visual content relevant to the requested modification rather than every visible detail. The result is a composed target description that should contain less irrelevant reference noise. Next comes the Anchor step. The system represents the reference image and the target description as comparable feature descriptions, then fuses them. The point is not to copy the reference wholesale. It is to strengthen useful semantics and supplement cues that the generated target description may have skipped. After anchoring, the Debias step estimates the visual semantic contribution of the reference image to the description. In everyday terms, it asks how much of the description is still explainable by the original image rather than by the desired edited target. That source contribution is added to the similarity calculation as a penalty term. Candidate images are then scored by a ranking rule that rewards closeness to the anchored target semantics while reducing credit for redundant reference-image influence. The output is a ranked list of target images, produced without task-specific training.
503.math: The main mathematical ideas are similarity scoring, feature fusion, and penalty-based debiasing. Similarity scoring means turning the query and each candidate image into descriptions that can be compared, then assigning higher rank to candidates judged closer to the desired target. The danger is that closeness is compressed into a number, so a candidate can appear close for the wrong reason: it may resemble the reference image rather than the modified target. Feature fusion is the Anchor step. It combines two evidence sources, reference-image features and generated target-description features, so missing but useful cues can be restored. The tradeoff is preservation versus contamination: the reference contains needed identity clues, but it also contains details that should stop mattering. The Debias step introduces a penalty term. A penalty is a deliberate subtraction from the score when a measured quantity represents an unwanted explanation. Here the unwanted quantity is the reference image's visual semantic contribution to the generated description when that contribution creates redundancy or bias. Mathematically, SDR-CIR changes ranking from one positive closeness measurement into a balanced score: reward target agreement, supplement omitted cues, and subtract source-driven bias. That fits composed retrieval because the task is not general similarity; it is similarity after a requested change.
503.dots: This paper sits in the repo's multimodal vision-language family because it makes image evidence and text instructions cooperate in one retrieval decision. It is also a similarity and ranking paper: the final act is scoring many candidate images and placing the most plausible targets near the top. Its closest siblings in the current JSON data are MCoT-MVS and XR, both also about composed image retrieval. MCoT-MVS uses reasoning cues to select patch-level and instance-level visual evidence before matching. XR splits the task across imagination, similarity, and question agents. SDR-CIR takes a different branch: it keeps the training-free reasoning setup but changes the score so source-image semantics can help and hurt in separate ways. The paper connects to a broader conference pattern where retrieval methods no longer trust a single closeness number. They add selection, verification, anchoring, or penalties because large candidate sets make false nearness costly at the top of the ranked list.
503.ww: The approach should work better than the naive description-and-search pipeline because it separates two effects that the naive score mixes together. Some source-image information is a legitimate anchor: without it, the generated target description may be too vague and candidates may satisfy the text while losing the source identity. Other source-image information is bias: it keeps the search attached to visual facts that the modification was supposed to change or ignore. Selective CoT helps at the source by asking the model to attend to modification-relevant visual content, which reduces irrelevant detail before any score is computed. The Anchor step then repairs under-description by adding useful reference cues back into the target representation. The Debias step guards against over-description by penalizing measured reference contribution in the similarity score. This push and pull matches the structure of composed retrieval. The user is asking for continuity plus change, so the ranking rule needs both a preserving force and a subtracting force. The abstract's experiments on three standard CIR benchmarks support the claim that this balance improves one-stage retrieval while keeping efficiency high.
503.po: The payoff is a training-free composed image retrieval method that can use a large multimodal model's reasoning without fully trusting its generated target description. Grounded in the abstract, SDR-CIR improves retrieval by supplementing omitted cues while suppressing redundant source-image influence. The reported result is state-of-the-art performance among one-stage methods on three standard CIR benchmarks, while maintaining high efficiency. Practically, this buys a more faithful visual search behavior: when a user gives an example image plus a modification, the system has an explicit way to keep helpful visual semantics, reduce misleading ones, and rank candidates by the edited intent rather than by raw resemblance to the source.
503.limits: The abstract does not provide the exact scoring formula, feature extractor details, prompt text, benchmark names in the truncated input file, or examples of failure cases, so those cannot be asserted from the per-paper input alone. The method assumes the multimodal language model can follow Selective CoT well enough to extract modification-relevant visual content. It also assumes the reference image's semantic contribution can be estimated accurately enough for a penalty to help rather than remove useful identity cues. Because the method is training-free, its quality may depend strongly on the underlying model and feature representations. Benchmark gains do not prove reliability for ambiguous edits, unusual image domains, adversarial prompts, or cases where the text describes a target attribute not visible or inferable from the reference.

504.bp: An e-commerce delivery estimate is a promise made before the package has finished moving. A customer uses it to decide whether the service is trustworthy; the platform uses it to plan operations and set expectations. The object being predicted is not a single mysterious number. It is the total time produced by a chain of concrete stages: the order is prepared, passed through logistics steps, moved across hops, and finally delivered. The paper argues that industry has mostly tried to improve this promise by building more complicated prediction models. That helps, but every new architecture is expensive to design, test, and deploy. EDTF asks a different question: can existing delivery-time models learn from the same data in a better way? Its answer is to change the training task itself, so the model learns ordered time ranges and checks whether local hop durations agree with the whole trip.
504.wh: The hard part is that delivery time has both a global face and a local face. The customer sees one end-to-end estimate, but the logistics system experiences many smaller durations. A model trained only to output one final number can miss that internal structure. It may learn that some features often go with longer or shorter deliveries, but it is not forced to understand how future hops add up into the final wait. Direct numerical prediction, called regression, also gives the model a sharp target: be close to this exact time. That can be awkward when delivery times are naturally ordered but noisy. Predicting twenty hours instead of twenty-one is much less wrong than predicting two hours instead of twenty-one, yet a plain number target does not by itself teach the model to preserve the ladder of time. The business pressure makes this worse: companies want faster iteration without rebuilding production models from scratch.
504.naive: A smart beginner would collect past orders, record features available before delivery, and train a model to predict the exact delivery time as one number. If the error is large, the beginner might build a bigger model or add more layers to capture more details. This fails in two ways suggested by the abstract. First, it treats time as a raw quantity instead of an ordered outcome where nearby ranges should be related. Second, it ignores the route-like composition of delivery: the total estimate should be compatible with the durations of the remaining hops. A model can look accurate on many examples while still learning an internally inconsistent story about the trip.
504.ap: EDTF's core move is to improve the learning process around an existing model rather than replace the model. It first changes the target from direct number guessing into ordered class prediction. Instead of asking only, "what exact time will this take?", the system asks the model to choose among time levels that keep their natural order. That makes the model learn that adjacent delivery ranges are closer than distant ones. Then EDTF gives the same prediction problem two views. One view is broad: the whole remaining delivery time from now to arrival. The other is narrow: the durations of future next-hop steps. The method trains these views to agree, using the fact that the sum of the future hop durations should match the overall estimated delivery time. This creates an extra teaching signal without adding new features.
504.mech: The input is the same kind of industrial delivery data that an estimated-time model already uses: records of delivery cases, their observed timing, and whatever features the existing model consumes. EDTF wraps around such a model as a plug-in training design. Step one is to take the original continuous delivery-time target and convert it into ordered categories. The exact category boundaries are not given in the abstract, so the supported claim is only that the categories preserve temporal order. The model then learns to place an example into the right ordered time region rather than only chasing one exact value. Step two is to split the learning signal into two related predictions. The macroscopic view predicts the whole end-to-end delivery time. The microscopic view predicts future next-hop durations, meaning the remaining small segments in the delivery process. Step three is a consistency check: add the predicted future hop durations together and compare that sum with the end-to-end estimate. When the two disagree, the training objective counts that disagreement as something to reduce. The output is still an estimated delivery time for the customer-facing task, but the model has been trained with both ordered time labels and an internal accounting rule that makes the route pieces cohere with the total.
504.math: Three mathematical ideas are doing the work. The first is ordinal classification: turning a number into ordered buckets while keeping the fact that bucket three is between bucket two and bucket four. This fits delivery time because time has a natural direction and nearby mistakes are not the same as far-away mistakes. The second is learning by reducing a defined error. EDTF changes what counts as wrong. The model is not judged only by distance from the final observed time; it is also judged by whether its small-step story agrees with its whole-trip story. The third idea is consistency across two views of the same object. In plain language, if a package still has several stages left, the predicted total wait should be compatible with the predicted waits for those stages. This is a self-supervised signal, meaning it is supervision created from the structure of the problem itself rather than from extra human labels or extra features. The tradeoff is precision versus learnability. Exact-time prediction asks for fine detail immediately. Ordered classes and cross-view agreement give the model a more structured path: learn the ladder of time and learn that parts should add to the whole.
504.dots: This paper sits near several recurring conference ideas even though its surface topic is delivery. It is a sequence and time problem because the future depends on an ordered process, not a flat pile of features. It is also an efficiency problem because the authors are not mainly selling a heavier architecture; they want a plug-in training change that can improve existing industrial models and reduce iteration cost. It connects to self-supervised learning through the consistency rule: the system creates an additional check from the relationship between hop durations and total duration. It also touches ranking-like thinking because ordinal prediction treats time ranges as ordered choices rather than unrelated labels. Compared with recommendation or retrieval papers that rank items for a user, EDTF ranks possible time regions for a delivery event. The shared deeper move is to use structure that already exists in the world, such as order, sequence, and agreement between views, so the learner is not left to infer everything from final labels alone.
504.ww: The method should help because it gives the model easier and more meaningful constraints than a bare final number. Ordered time categories soften the target while preserving the important direction of the mistake. If the correct arrival falls in a medium-late range, the model is encouraged to treat nearby ranges as related and distant ranges as very different. That matches how delivery promises are used: being slightly off is less damaging than confusing same-day delivery with a much later arrival. The cross-view rule adds a second source of discipline. A model that predicts a short total time while also predicting long remaining hops is telling two incompatible stories. Penalizing that mismatch pushes the internal representation, meaning the model's compressed description of the delivery case, toward facts that are useful at both scales. This is why the abstract says convergence accelerates: the learner receives more structured feedback per example. It does not merely wait for final error to reveal a problem; it can also notice when its local and global timing views contradict each other.
504.po: The practical payoff is a way to improve estimated delivery time accuracy without forcing a company to redesign its prediction model every time. EDTF is described as plug-and-play, so the intended value is that existing models can keep their architecture while receiving a richer learning objective. The abstract reports experiments on a large-scale industrial dataset and says the method consistently enhances performance and speeds convergence across five diverse models, though the input text cuts off before naming them. For an e-commerce platform, the useful capability is sharper customer-facing time promises and faster deployment cycles.
504.limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The delivery process must have meaningful next-hop structure, and the data must record or support learning those future hop durations well enough for the consistency signal to be useful. The ordered time categories must be chosen sensibly; poor buckets could hide important timing differences. The abstract says no extra features are needed, but it does not prove the method works when routes, warehouses, or customer behavior change sharply. It also reports industrial experiments but, in the provided input, the sentence is truncated before the full list of model settings and metrics appears.

505.bp: The paper is about putting useful machine learning models onto small Web of Things devices: sensors, controllers, cameras, wearables, and other connected machines that cannot carry a large server-sized model. The practical need is simple. A device at the edge should make a local decision without always sending data elsewhere, but it has strict memory limits. Designers therefore need a model shape that is accurate enough and small enough at the same time. Neural architecture search, meaning automated trial and selection of model designs, already helps by exploring many possible layer layouts. EdgeGen starts from the observation that size is not only decided by the layout. It is also decided by how model numbers are stored. Quantization stores those numbers with fewer bits, like using a shorter ruler with coarser markings. A larger design that looks too big before compression may fit after quantization and may be more accurate than a tiny uncompressed design.
505.wh: The hard part is that the best edge model is hidden inside a combined choice: the model architecture and the quantization method applied to it. If search treats these as separate stages, it can reject useful candidates too early. A large architecture may violate the memory limit when measured in ordinary high-precision numbers, but the same architecture may fit once its weights are stored with fewer bits. The search space also grows quickly. Every model design can be paired with several compression choices, so the number of possibilities becomes too large for slow exhaustive testing. The abstract names a second pressure: evaluation itself is costly. To know whether a candidate is worth keeping, the system needs an accuracy estimate in a short time. On edge devices, full training or full evaluation for each candidate would consume the very resources the paper is trying to save.
505.naive: A smart beginner would first run ordinary architecture search, pick a small model that satisfies the memory budget, and then quantize it afterward. This seems natural because it divides the problem into two clean steps: find a compact design, then compress it. The failure is that the first step has already narrowed the world too much. It only considers models that fit before compression, so it ignores larger candidates that would fit after compression and might preserve more useful prediction power. Another beginner solution is to test many architecture-and-quantization pairs directly. That fails because each evaluation takes time, and the paired search space is vast.
505.ap: EdgeGen's central move is to make quantization part of the search itself. Instead of asking only, "Which architecture should we use?" it asks, "Which architecture, together with which way of storing its numbers more compactly, should we use?" That changes the search from a layout problem into a joint design-and-compression problem. To keep this expanded search from becoming unmanageable, the paper uses multi-beam Monte Carlo Tree Search. In plain terms, it grows several promising paths through a decision tree, uses partly random exploration to avoid staring only at the first good-looking option, and keeps multiple candidates alive at once. A constraint validator checks whether a candidate satisfies the memory requirement. A graph neural network based performance predictor, meaning a learned estimator that reads the model as connected parts, gives a quick prediction of model quality.
505.mech: The input is a device setting with a memory constraint, plus a space of possible neural network architectures and several quantization methods. EdgeGen treats model construction as a sequence of decisions. One decision may choose a structural part of the network; another may choose how the model's numbers will be represented after quantization. These decisions form a tree: each branch is a partial model choice, and a full path is a complete candidate. Multi-beam Monte Carlo Tree Search explores this tree by keeping several active beams, or promising partial paths, rather than committing to one path too early. At each stage, it expands candidate branches, samples possibilities to learn which areas look fruitful, and uses accumulated evidence to decide where to spend more search effort. The constraint validator then acts as a hard gate. It checks whether a proposed original or quantized model can satisfy the memory budget, so impossible candidates do not waste expensive evaluation time. For candidates that pass this gate, EdgeGen uses a GNN-based performance predictor. The model architecture is naturally a graph of connected operations, so the predictor can read that structure and estimate how well the candidate is likely to perform without fully training every option. The output is a selected model design, paired with a quantization method, intended to meet the edge constraint while retaining high accuracy.
505.math: The main mathematical idea is search under constraints. Search means choosing from many possible designs; a constraint is a rule that cannot be broken, here the memory limit of an edge device. EdgeGen also uses a tradeoff calculation: accuracy versus memory, and search quality versus search time. Quantization is a numerical compression idea. A model normally stores many numbers with fine precision. Quantization stores them using fewer possible values, which saves memory but can blur small distinctions. The risk is that too much rounding damages the model's decisions; the opportunity is that a larger structure may survive this rounding better than a smaller uncompressed one. Monte Carlo Tree Search is a way to explore a branching decision problem when checking every branch is impossible. "Monte Carlo" means using sampled trials to estimate which branches are promising; the tree represents sequential design choices. Multi-beam search keeps several promising paths alive, balancing local commitment with wider exploration. The performance predictor adds graph learning: the model design is read as nodes and links, where operations and their connections carry evidence about likely performance. This fits because a neural architecture is not just a list of parts; the way parts connect changes what the model can compute.
505.dots: This paper sits in the conference's efficiency and scalability family because the central pressure is scarce resource budget: memory on edge devices and time during search. It connects to ranking because the system must sort many candidate models by expected usefulness under a hard constraint. It connects to probability through tree search, where sampled evidence guides belief about which unexplored branches are worth trying. It connects to graph learning because the performance predictor treats an architecture as connected components rather than as a flat name. Neighboring papers in the same batch show the same deeper pattern under different surfaces. The delivery-time paper improves deployment by changing the learning objective instead of only building larger models. The adaptive graph-pruning paper in the efficiency family also asks how to spend computation only where it is likely to help. EdgeGen is the architecture-search version of that broader question: how do we choose a small useful object from a huge pile without measuring every object fully?
505.ww: EdgeGen should work better than the naive pipeline because it changes when compression is considered. If quantization is postponed until the end, the search is blind to designs whose value appears only after compression. By placing quantization inside the search space, EdgeGen can compare two candidates in the form they will actually have on the device, not in an unrealistic pre-compression form. The constraint validator helps because memory feasibility is not a soft preference in edge deployment; a model either fits or it does not. Rejecting infeasible candidates early saves evaluation time for plausible ones. The tree search helps because the space is too large for a complete sweep, but not so chaotic that every trial is independent. Partial architecture choices give clues about future candidates, and sampled exploration can use those clues. The graph-based predictor helps for the same reason: connected model parts often reveal likely behavior before full training. Together these pieces spend search effort on candidates that are both physically deployable and likely to be accurate.
505.po: The payoff is a more practical way to generate models for Web of Things devices. EdgeGen can find larger quantized models that satisfy strict memory constraints, a class of solutions ordinary architecture-only search may miss. The abstract reports that it searches both original and quantized models efficiently, uses a fast performance predictor, and consistently beats prior neural architecture search methods across multiple tests. For a developer, the useful capability is less manual trial and error: the search can consider compression and architecture together, then return a model meant for the actual resource-limited device rather than for an ideal machine.
505.limits: Several assumptions must hold. Quantization must preserve enough useful signal for the chosen model; if rounding the model numbers destroys the needed distinctions, a larger compressed design may not help. The performance predictor must also be trustworthy for the architectures and quantization methods being searched. If it has learned from examples unlike the target device or target task, it may rank candidates poorly. The abstract does not prove how EdgeGen behaves under every hardware type, latency constraint, energy budget, or sensor workload. It emphasizes memory constraints and reported test performance, but the excerpt does not show detailed failure cases or the cost of building the predictor itself.

506.bp: Large web collections are no longer just pages of words. A news post, social post, product page, or media article may carry its meaning through text and images together. The practical need is to organize that flood into topics people can inspect: not only "sports" or "politics," but clusters of words and pictures that point to the same underlying subject. Topic modeling is the old name for this organizing task: given many documents, find recurring themes that explain why some documents belong together. This paper asks how to do that when a document has both written and visual evidence. Its starting point is that modern neural topic models, especially ones built around variational autoencoders, have worked well for text but are weak for mixed web media. MM-vNTM is proposed as a web-scale topic discovery method that treats text and images as jointly informative and tries to make the discovered topics coherent and interpretable.
506.wh: The hard part is that text and images are different kinds of evidence. A caption can name an event, while a picture can show people, objects, style, or setting without naming them. If the system treats only the text as real evidence, it misses visual meaning. If it merely bolts image features onto a text model, the two channels may not agree about what the topic is. The abstract names two failures. Posterior collapse means the model's hidden document summary becomes ignored or uninformative; the output can be produced without using the intended topic structure, so the learned topics become weak. The second failure is missing directional semantics. In plain terms, many text and image representations carry meaning in their direction, like arrows pointing toward concepts, more than in their raw length. A model that ignores this arrow-like structure can group items by the wrong kind of closeness, producing incoherent topics and making the result hard to interpret.
506.naive: A smart beginner would start by running an ordinary text topic model on the words and, if images are available, attach an image description or image feature afterward. Another simple attempt would average the text and image descriptions into one mixed document vector and cluster those averages. These ideas fail because the agreement between words and pictures is the main problem, not a cleanup step. A web post's image may reinforce the text, add a missing clue, or point in a different direction. Averaging can wash out that structure. A plain neural topic model can also collapse, meaning its learned hidden topic signal stops carrying useful information. The beginner gets groups, but the groups may contain words and images that do not form topics a person can understand.
506.ap: The paper's central move is to put both modalities, text and images, into a shared rounded space where direction is the main evidence of meaning. MM-vNTM starts from pre-aligned cross-modal embeddings, meaning existing numeric descriptions where related text and image evidence have already been placed into a comparable coordinate system. It then jointly models document-level representations from both modalities in a shared hyperspherical latent space. A hypersphere is the surface of a high-dimensional ball; using it emphasizes where a point points rather than how long the point is. The method also defines topics as mixtures of von Mises-Fisher distributions in an L2-normalized word embedding space. In everyday language, each topic is not just a bag of frequent words. It is a cluster of directions around one or more preferred semantic arrows, so words and documents can be grouped by directional similarity.
506.mech: The input is a multimedia web dataset: many documents, each with textual data and image data. The first step is to represent both channels with pre-aligned cross-modal embeddings. An embedding is a compact numeric description; here, pre-aligned means text and image descriptions have already been arranged so related meanings can be compared across channels. For each document, MM-vNTM builds document-level representations for the text side and the image side. Instead of treating those as separate topic sources, it models them jointly in one shared hyperspherical latent space, a hidden representation space shaped like the surface of a sphere. That choice matters because all points are effectively compared by direction after normalization, reducing the role of raw magnitude. Next, the model defines the topics themselves as mixtures of von Mises-Fisher distributions. A von Mises-Fisher distribution is a probability pattern on a sphere: it says points are more likely when their directions lie near a central direction. A mixture means a topic can be represented by several such directional concentrations rather than one rigid center. The system then learns which directional topic components explain the normalized word representations and the multimodal document representations. What comes out is a set of discovered topics and document-topic assignments meant to organize web media while keeping the topics readable.
506.math: The mathematical core is probability on directions. Ordinary topic modeling asks: if a document is about some hidden topics, what words would those topics tend to produce? A neural topic model learns this through examples by defining a hidden document summary and training it to reconstruct observed text. A variational autoencoder is a way to learn such a hidden summary when the exact topic mixture is not directly observed: it guesses a compact hidden description, uses it to rebuild the document evidence, and adjusts the guess so rebuilding improves. The danger, posterior collapse, happens when the hidden description stops mattering. MM-vNTM adds geometry that fits the evidence better. L2-normalization rescales vectors so their length is fixed; after that, their direction carries the comparison. A hyperspherical latent space is a shared surface where document meanings from text and images can be compared as directions. The von Mises-Fisher distribution is like a bell-shaped probability cloud wrapped around that sphere, concentrated around a central arrow. A mixture of such clouds lets a topic cover several related semantic directions. The tradeoff is interpretability versus compression: reducing web media to directions makes large-scale grouping practical, but fine details not captured by those directions can disappear.
506.dots: This paper sits squarely inside the repo's multimodal vision-language family: it tries to make unlike evidence cooperate before a system organizes or scores anything. It is also a similarity paper because the decisive measurement is directional closeness among normalized text, image, word, and document representations. Nearby papers in the same batch show the same pressure with different outputs. SDR-CIR uses image and text together to rank target images after a requested change. Cross-view geo-localization aligns ground-level and satellite images so two views of one place can be matched. Meme engagement analysis combines visual novelty with textual emotion to study social response. MM-vNTM applies the shared idea to topic discovery rather than retrieval, localization, or engagement prediction. Its sibling problem is not choosing one best item from a collection; it is carving the whole collection into human-readable subject regions. Across these papers, the deeper question is how to preserve the evidence that survives across modalities without letting one channel erase or distort the other.
506.ww: The method should work better than a plain text topic model because many web topics are expressed partly outside the words. If images and text have already been pre-aligned, then related visual and written clues can support the same document-level topic estimate. The hyperspherical choice helps because the abstract says both text and images carry directional semantics. When meaning is mostly about the direction of a representation, fixing vector length and comparing directions is a cleaner language than comparing raw coordinates. The vMF mixture then gives the model a probability rule that matches that geometry: points near a topic direction receive more support, and points farther around the sphere receive less. This can reduce incoherence because a topic is encouraged to gather words and document evidence that point toward related meanings, not merely words that co-occur by accident. It can also fight posterior collapse by making the hidden topic structure geometrically tied to the observed normalized word space and the joint document representations. The abstract's experiments report consistently better overall topic quality than unimodal and multimodal baselines on multimedia web datasets.
506.po: The payoff is a topic discovery system designed for real web media rather than text-only collections. Grounded in the abstract, MM-vNTM buys three capabilities: it uses both text and image evidence, it models document meanings in a shared spherical space, and it defines topics through directional probability mixtures that aim to improve coherence and interpretability. The reported experimental result is that it consistently beats state-of-the-art unimodal and multimodal baselines in overall topic quality on multimedia web datasets. Practically, that means a large web collection can be organized into topics that better reflect how modern content actually communicates, with images and words contributing to the same discovered structure.
506.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The pre-aligned cross-modal embeddings must already place related text and image evidence into a trustworthy shared comparison system; if that alignment is biased or noisy, MM-vNTM inherits the error. The method assumes directional similarity is the right clue for both modalities and for word meanings. It also assumes topic quality metrics and multimedia web datasets reflect the interpretability people need in real browsing or analysis settings. The abstract does not prove how the method behaves when images contradict text, when documents contain many unrelated images, when visual evidence is culturally ambiguous, or when web-scale deployment costs dominate topic quality.

507.bp: A recommender is trying to answer a human question that is rarely spoken directly: given what this person has done before, what item should appear next? For shopping-like domains such as sports goods, beauty products, and toys, the record may contain purchases or clicks, but the underlying interest is richer than the record. A person who bought running shoes may care about trail running, injury prevention, a brand, a price range, or a gift for someone else. This paper serves the part of recommendation where large language models are used as interpreters of meaning, not only as text generators. The need arises because item attributes and behavior logs are incomplete clues. The paper argues that a user's visible item choices should be read at two levels: the person's own explicit interests and the less visible interests suggested by similar groups of users. Its practical goal is to generate recommendations from a more complete account of what the user may want.
507.wh: The hard part is that user interest is both personal and social. A user's own history is the strongest evidence, but it is often short, narrow, accidental, or mixed across several motives. Similar users can add missing evidence, yet groups can also blur people together and make the system chase the crowd. The abstract says recent LLM-based recommenders already build and combine semantic descriptions of users and items. That helps because text-like item attributes can reveal meaning beyond raw item IDs. But semantic integration alone still treats the available descriptions as things to merge, rather than as clues that should be reasoned through. The paper's tension is therefore two-sided: individual behavior tells the system what this person explicitly touched, while group behavior hints at interests this person has not yet revealed. The challenge is to let these two sources correct each other without letting either one dominate.
507.naive: A smart beginner would list the items a user interacted with, ask an LLM to summarize those items into a user profile, and then recommend items whose attributes sound close to that profile. A slightly stronger version would find users with similar profiles and borrow their favorite items. This fails because it makes the reasoning too flat. Item attributes are not always already meaningful; the system may need to infer features from them. Similarity between users is also not a fixed fact before the user descriptions are cleaned up. If group profiles are built from weak individual profiles, they inherit those mistakes. If individual profiles are updated from crude groups, they may become generic. The simple pipeline has no disciplined loop for improving both levels together.
507.ap: The core idea is to make recommendation a back-and-forth reasoning process between items, users, and groups. The paper's ISRF method first asks the language model to reason over item attributes in both directions and through several steps, so item features are inferred rather than merely copied. Those semantic item features support a semantic interaction graph, a relationship map that records which users show explicit interest in which item meanings. Next, the method builds semantic user features and connects similar users in a user graph, so group interests can be inferred from neighborhoods of related users. Finally, it repeats the refinement in batches: individual explicit interests directly reshape group implicit interests, and group implicit interests indirectly improve the description of each individual. The important move is iteration. The system does not freeze the individual profile before group reasoning; it lets the two levels become progressively more consistent.
507.mech: The input is a record of historical user behaviors, item attributes, and the task of generating relevant items for a user. First, the method turns raw item attributes into semantic item features. In plain terms, it asks what the attributes imply about the item, then reasons back from possible meanings to the attributes to keep the interpretation tied to evidence. This multi-step bidirectional reasoning is meant to produce item descriptions that carry more useful meaning than a shallow attribute list. Second, the method builds a semantic interaction graph. The nodes are users and item-level meanings, and the links express explicit interests: this user interacted with items carrying these inferred features. Third, it generates semantic user features from the item features attached to each user's behavior. These user descriptions become the basis for a similarity-based user graph, where links connect users whose inferred interests are close enough to treat as group evidence. Fourth, the method infers implicit group interests from those neighborhoods. Fifth, it runs iterative batch optimization, meaning it defines a mismatch to reduce across a batch of users and repeatedly adjusts the individual and group descriptions. The output is a refined user-interest account that can guide a generative recommender toward items that match both the user's visible history and the group patterns that history suggests.
507.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing work here. The first is representation, meaning a rich object is turned into a structured description that a model can compare. The paper uses semantic features for items and users: not just identifiers, but descriptions of what the items and users seem to mean. The second idea is graph reasoning. A graph is a map of things and links. Here, one graph connects users to item meanings through explicit behavior, and another connects users to similar users. The reason graphs fit is that interest is not isolated inside one record; evidence can travel from items to users and from users to related users. The third idea is similarity, the act of deciding which differences matter enough to separate users and which can be ignored. This is risky because two users can look close for the wrong reason, so the similarity graph depends on good semantic user features. The fourth idea is optimization, which here means defining what counts as inconsistent or inaccurate interest reasoning and changing the model's descriptions to reduce that error over batches. The tradeoff is personalization versus group smoothing: the method wants group evidence to fill gaps without erasing individual taste.
507.dots: This paper sits inside the recommender-systems family, where many papers try to choose a small useful set from a large item pile under incomplete evidence. It connects directly to similarity because the user graph works only if closeness between user descriptions captures real shared interest rather than surface overlap. It connects to network reasoning because the method treats interactions and similar-user links as roads along which evidence can move. It also connects to ranking and generative recommendation: the final user-interest account is useful only if it changes which candidate items rise to the top or are generated for the user. Compared with ordinary LLM recommendation, the paper is not just asking the language model to summarize text. It asks the model to support a chain from item attributes to individual explicit interests to group implicit interests, then back into individual modeling. That places it among 2026 work concerned with repairing the comparison before making the recommendation.
507.ww: The method should help when two conditions hold: item attributes contain interpretable clues, and similar users really do reveal missing parts of one another's interests. The individual layer protects the system from pure herd behavior because each user's explicit history directly guides the group-interest refinement. The group layer protects the system from sparse or narrow personal histories because similar users can supply signals the target user has not yet shown. The back-and-forth loop matters because early descriptions are likely imperfect. Better item features make better user features; better user features make the similarity graph more trustworthy; a better similarity graph makes group interests less noisy; better group interests then improve individual modeling. This is a controlled form of evidence sharing. Instead of making one pass from behavior to profile to recommendation, ISRF repeatedly checks whether the personal and group stories agree. That can produce more comprehensive interest learning than a flat summary, especially when a user's real preference is only partly visible in past behavior.
507.po: The payoff is a recommender that can use LLM-derived meaning without stopping at individual semantic summaries. The abstract reports that ISRF enables more accurate and comprehensive user interest learning and that experiments on Sports, Beauty, and Toys datasets outperform strong baselines. Grounded in the abstract, the claimed capability is not merely better item text processing. It is a richer bridge between what a user explicitly did and what similar-user groups imply. For a deployed recommender, that means the system may recover interests that are plausible but not yet obvious from one user's history alone, while still keeping the individual's observed behavior in the loop.
507.limits: The abstract does not prove that the inferred group interests are always real interests rather than shared exposure, popularity, or platform-driven behavior. It assumes item attributes are rich enough for useful semantic reasoning and that the LLM's inferred features are faithful to those attributes. It also assumes user similarity built from semantic features reflects meaningful preference, not accidental overlap. The reported evidence comes from Sports, Beauty, and Toys datasets, so the claim may not transfer unchanged to domains with sensitive choices, fast-changing intent, sparse attributes, or strong social pressure. The abstract names iterative batch optimization but does not specify the exact objective, failure cases, cost, or how much group reasoning can override individual signals.

508.bp: An Ethereum node is useful only if it can hear from the wider network. It learns about blocks, transactions, and peers by keeping network connections open to other nodes. An eclipse attack turns that social fact into a security failure: instead of breaking Ethereum's cryptography, the attacker surrounds one target node with attacker-controlled neighbors until the target's view of the chain comes only through hostile doors. The paper studies whether that can be done against post-Merge Ethereum execution-layer nodes, where the practical details differ from earlier Bitcoin and Monero studies. The real system being protected is the peer-to-peer layer that lets a decentralized chain stay decentralized in practice. If a node can be isolated when it restarts, then honest consensus rules may still run, but the node is making decisions from a curated false neighborhood. This work matters because decentralization depends not just on many nodes existing, but on honest nodes being able to find and keep honest connections.
508.wh: The hard part is that a peer-to-peer network must be open enough for strangers to find one another. A new or restarted node cannot already know every good peer, so it relies on discovery tables, public peer lists, and available incoming slots. Those conveniences are also attack surfaces. If the system accepts unsolicited discovery information too freely, an attacker can plant bad addresses before the node chooses neighbors. If official peer lists are built by a crawler, then influencing what the crawler sees can influence what later nodes trust as a starting map. If nodes have limited incoming slots, filling or steering those slots changes which connections remain possible. The defender wants openness, reachability, and low coordination cost; the attacker wants to convert those same mechanisms into a controlled funnel. The post-Merge setting makes the question empirical: known attacks against Bitcoin or Monero do not automatically prove the same path works against Ethereum execution-layer clients.
508.naive: A smart beginner would try to protect Ethereum nodes by checking whether peers speak the protocol correctly and by letting each node keep many connections. That sounds reasonable because an eclipse attacker cannot isolate a node unless the target accepts attacker peers. The failure is that correctness at the message level is not the same as diversity at the neighborhood level. A malicious peer can speak valid protocol messages while still being part of a surrounding wall. The beginner might also trust bootstrap and DNS-based peer lists because they are official sources, but the paper shows those lists can be influenced through the process that builds them. Finally, adding slots does not help if the network's idle capacity is already scarce or if attackers can occupy the reachable spaces first.
508.ap: The paper's core idea is to treat node isolation as a multi-stage control problem over how Ethereum nodes find and keep peers. The attack does not rely on one magic packet. It first poisons the target's discovery table by sending unsolicited messages, so the target's local memory of possible peers becomes attacker-heavy. It then reaches upstream into Ethereum's DNS-based peerlist by identifying and manipulating the official DNS crawler, so the public starting list can also contain attacker influence. Finally, it hijacks idle incoming connection slots across the network to prevent benign peers from filling the spaces that would rescue the target's view. The target moment is restart, because a restarting node rebuilds its peer neighborhood and is especially dependent on bootstrap logic. The contribution is an end-to-end implementation showing that these pieces can be chained against Ethereum 2.0 execution-layer nodes, not just described as separate weaknesses.
508.mech: The mechanism begins with a target Ethereum execution-layer node and the network machinery it uses to regain peers after restart. First, the attacker prepares addresses under attacker control. The abstract says the DNS list poisoning phase needs only 28 IP addresses over 100 days, so this is not framed as a massive address-flooding attack. Second, the attacker sends unsolicited discovery messages that alter the target's discovery table. That table is the target's local address book: when the node needs peers, entries in that book affect who it may try. Third, the attacker works on the broader bootstrap source. Ethereum uses a DNS-based peerlist, and the paper says the attack identifies and manipulates the official DNS crawler. In practical terms, the crawler is a collector whose observations become a public list; influencing the collector can make hostile entries appear as ordinary candidates. Fourth, the attacker occupies idle incoming connection slots across the network. A slot is a scarce opening where a node can accept a connection. By hijacking idle slots, the attacker reduces the chance that benign peers can enter the relevant connection pattern and undo the isolation. Fifth, when the target restarts and seeks peers, these poisoned sources and occupied slots steer it toward attacker-controlled neighbors. The output is not stolen keys or rewritten consensus rules; it is a node whose network view is fully isolated even while protocol messages may look ordinary.
508.math: The main mathematical object is a network map. The nodes are Ethereum machines, and the links are peer-to-peer connections through which block and transaction information can travel. An eclipse attack changes the map around one chosen node so nearly every road out of that node leads to the attacker. The paper also uses scarcity reasoning. Each node has a limited number of connection slots, so occupying a slot is like reserving a seat before an honest participant arrives. Once slots are scarce, the security question becomes a matching problem under hostile pressure: which peers get paired with which openings, and who controls the candidate pool? There is also probability in the measurements. A redirection success rate of 45% or 95% is an estimate from repeated attempts, not a moral label; it measures how often the steering process sends outgoing choices where the attacker wants. The DNS crawler phase is a sampling problem. A crawler observes part of the network and turns those observations into a list others may use. If the sample is manipulable, the list can become a biased map. The key tradeoff is openness versus resistance to capture. Ethereum needs lightweight discovery so nodes can join, but every open path must decide how much influence an unsolicited message, a crawler observation, or an occupied slot should have.
508.dots: This paper sits directly in the repo's privacy and security family because it studies a boundary where useful sharing becomes an attack path. The shared signal is peer information: nodes must share addresses and accept connections, but attackers can shape that sharing until it leaks control over a target's neighborhood. It also belongs to the network concept. Like graph-mining papers that ask when links carry trustworthy evidence, this work asks when links lie. Here the link is not a recommendation edge or a knowledge-base relation; it is a live network connection that determines what a blockchain node can see. The paper is adjacent to blockchain optimization work such as DAG tuning and cross-shard scheduling because all of them treat blockchain systems as connected infrastructure with scarce communication capacity. The difference is adversarial intent. Optimization papers try to route work faster under changing load; this paper shows that peer-management rules can be optimized by an attacker to reduce the target's honest connectivity.
508.ww: The attack should work when the target's restart behavior depends heavily on the exact sources the attacker has shaped. A restarted node is vulnerable because it is rebuilding its view from saved discovery state, bootstrap lists, and available network openings. If the discovery table contains many attacker addresses, the first candidate pool is already biased. If the DNS-based peerlist has also been influenced, the supposedly independent public starting point is less independent than it appears. If benign incoming slots are hard to obtain because idle capacity is scarce or occupied, honest peers have fewer chances to dilute the attacker's neighborhood. These stages reinforce one another. Poisoning only the local table might fail if a clean DNS list or honest incoming connections refresh the node's view. Poisoning only a public list might fail if the node has enough diverse local peers. Slot hijacking alone might not choose the target's outgoing peers. Combined, they attack the address book, the public directory, and the capacity market at the same time. That is why the abstract's jump from 45% to 95% outgoing redirection success matters: it suggests the slot stage closes an escape route left by weaker steering.
508.po: The payoff is a concrete test of a threat that had been clearer for other cryptocurrencies than for Ethereum after the Merge. The paper provides the first end-to-end implementation against Ethereum 2.0 execution-layer nodes, validates it on the Sepolia testnet, and supports severity with broader mainnet measurements. The reported numbers make the result operational rather than merely theoretical: DNS list poisoning can be done with 28 IP addresses over 100 days, slot hijacking raises outgoing redirection success from 45% to 95%, and more than 80% of public nodes lack enough idle capacity for effective benign slot occupation. The practical capability is a clearer basis for hardening Ethereum peer discovery and peer management.
508.limits: The claims depend on the studied Ethereum execution-layer behavior, especially restart-time bootstrapping and peer management. If clients change discovery-table rules, DNS crawler behavior, slot policies, or diversity checks, the attack path may change. The abstract reports controlled Sepolia experiments and broad mainnet measurements, but it does not prove that every deployment, private node, client implementation, or future protocol version has the same exposure. The countermeasures are only mentioned, not described in the provided input, so their cost and completeness cannot be assessed here. The attack also demonstrates network isolation, not every possible downstream consequence; what an isolated node can be made to accept or miss depends on surrounding consensus, monitoring, and recovery behavior.

509.bp: A paid ad-free subscription sounds like a simple bargain: the user gives the platform money, and in return the platform no longer needs to watch the user for advertising. This paper asks whether that bargain changes the data pipeline in practice. The setting is familiar large social platforms, specifically Instagram, Facebook, and X, where the ad-based business model has long made user tracking seem commercially useful. Under the GDPR, removing advertising as a purpose should matter because data collection is supposed to be tied to a stated need, kept limited to that need, and explained clearly. The paper studies the gap between three things: what the paid product seems to promise, what platform data exports show is still retained or collected, and what users believe should happen. The real object is not a model accuracy score; it is the trust boundary between a platform, a payment choice, and the private traces users leave behind.
509.wh: The problem is hard because data collection has more than one possible explanation. If a platform still records ad-related data after a user pays for an ad-free tier, that looks inconsistent with the idea that ads justified the collection. But platforms can answer that data also supports personalization, product improvement, safety, or other experience features. The same stored field can therefore sit inside several stories: advertising infrastructure, user preference memory, security logging, or service improvement. Users cannot inspect this directly from the product screen. They see fewer ads, but they do not see whether the underlying collection machinery changed. Legal principles such as purpose limitation, data minimization, and transparency are also harder to evaluate than a visible interface change. The paper has to compare evidence from platform exports with user expectations, because either side alone would be incomplete: exports show practice, while surveys show what people understand and normatively expect from the paid option.
509.naive: A smart beginner would compare the product labels. One tier has ads, one tier says ad-free, so the beginner might assume the second tier switches off ad-targeting collection and keeps only the data needed to run the service. That fails because the label describes what the user sees, not necessarily what the platform stores. Another beginner move would be to read the platform's general policy and decide whether the practice is acceptable from written claims. That also fails because broad policy language may not reveal what specific records remain in a user's export. The paper instead treats the question as an empirical privacy audit: inspect data exports and separately ask users what they expect and what they believe actually happens.
509.ap: The central move is to split a vague privacy promise into measurable pieces. First, the authors look at data exports from three major platforms to see whether ad-related data continues to appear under ad-free subscriptions. That turns an invisible backend practice into something that can be inspected. Second, they survey 255 Prolific participants to separate two kinds of belief. One is normative expectation: what users think should happen when they pay for ad-free service. The other is descriptive expectation: what users think platforms will actually do. This distinction matters because a skeptical user may believe platforms will keep collecting data while still thinking they ought to collect less. By comparing retained data, expected reduction, and skeptical belief, the paper identifies a mismatch rather than merely saying users are confused or platforms are unclear.
509.mech: The mechanism begins with one concrete comparison: ad-free versus ad-based subscription models. The paper asks whether the change in payment and advertising status is matched by a change in data collection practice. The first input is platform data exports from Instagram, Facebook, and X. These exports are treated as evidence of what the platform retains or collects about a user. The authors examine them for ad-related data that persists even when the subscription is ad-free. The output of that part is a practice-side finding: the platforms continue to retain or collect some ad-related data in ad-free subscriptions. The second input is a survey of 255 Prolific participants. The survey separates what participants think should happen from what they think actually happens. The authors then count the responses: 69 percent normatively expect data collection to be reduced, while 63 percent believe platforms would still collect about the same amount of data. The final comparison lines up three columns: observed export evidence, user privacy expectations, and user skepticism. If many users expect less collection, many also doubt platforms will provide it, and exports still show ad-related data, then the central result is a documented disconnect between visible product change, platform data practice, and user understanding.
509.math: The main mathematical idea is measurement under opacity. The platform's internal collection system is not directly visible to users, so the study uses observable traces as a proxy: exported records stand in for retained or collected data. The mathematical move is not a complicated formula; it is disciplined comparison. First define two groups or conditions, ad-free and ad-based service, then ask which kinds of records should differ if advertising is no longer a justification. Second, count user beliefs in a survey population. A percentage is a compact summary of repeated answers: 69 out of every 100 similar respondents, in this sample, say collection should be reduced; 63 out of every 100 believe platforms will still collect about the same amount. Third, compare expectation with practice. This is a causal-looking question, but the abstract supports it as an empirical alignment study, not proof that the subscription alone caused every retained field. The paper also uses the logic of information minimization: if a purpose disappears, the amount and type of collected information should shrink. The tradeoff is personalization versus privacy. Personalization benefits from remembering more about a user, while privacy principles ask whether each remembered detail has a necessary, transparent purpose.
509.dots: This paper sits with platform privacy, security measurement, and responsible web governance papers because it studies what happens at a boundary users cannot inspect. It connects to privacy work by asking what useful signal is allowed to cross from the user's behavior into the platform's long-term records, and what should stop crossing once ads are removed. It connects to information measurement because the evidence is not the platform's promise but the remaining records in data exports and the counted responses from users. It also connects to causality and policy evaluation: the question is whether changing the business model from ad-based to paid ad-free should change data practices, and whether continued collection can still be justified by another purpose such as personalization. Neighboring work on platform trust, transparency, and online harms faces the same hidden-structure problem. Users experience an interface, while the consequential decision often happens in logging, ranking, retention, or backend data use.
509.ww: The approach works because it avoids treating privacy as only a matter of stated policy or user feeling. Data exports give a more concrete window into practice than a product name or marketing description. They do not reveal everything, but they show records that platforms make available about a user, including whether some ad-related traces remain. The survey adds a different kind of evidence: whether the paid ad-free model carries a privacy meaning for users. The split between normative and descriptive expectations is especially useful. If users merely expected less collection and also believed platforms delivered it, the issue might be framed as possible compliance. If users merely distrusted platforms without a stated expectation, the issue might be framed as cynicism. Here the two numbers together show a sharper tension: many participants think collection should fall, and many think it probably will not. When that is paired with export evidence of continued ad-related data, the paper can argue that the mismatch is structural, not just a misunderstanding by one side.
509.po: The payoff is a clearer way to evaluate paid ad-free subscriptions as privacy products, not just advertising products. The paper shows that removing visible ads does not necessarily mean removing ad-related data collection or retention. It grounds that claim in exports from Instagram, Facebook, and X, and it grounds the user side in a 255-person survey. The result is useful for regulators, platform designers, and users because it points to a specific compliance pressure: if a platform keeps collecting data after the advertising purpose is removed, it must explain the purpose, minimize the data, and make the practice transparent.
509.limits: The abstract supports a careful empirical claim, not a complete audit of every internal database or every platform. Data exports show what is exposed through export tools, which may not equal all retained data or all backend uses. The three platforms are major examples, but they do not prove the same pattern for every ad-free service. The survey has 255 Prolific participants, so its percentages describe that sample and similar respondents, not all users everywhere. The abstract also does not prove whether each retained ad-related field violates GDPR; it raises compliance questions around purpose limitation, data minimization, and transparency.
